opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I love that example, partly because it's such a clean illustration of the core problem we're worried about with scalable oversight.

If you read Caro's *The Power Broker*, one of the striking things is that Moses was, by all accounts, the best bill drafter in Albany. He understood the law in more detail than the legislators voting on it. He'd write these very long, technical bills, and buried in them would be a clause that looked innocuous. The famous one is the Triborough Bridge Authority. The bond covenants were written so that the authority's powers were tied to the bonds, and he could keep issuing new bonds. That effectively made his position permanent, because the state couldn't remove him without impairing a contract with bondholders, which runs into constitutional problems. The legislators had every opportunity to read it. It was right there in the text. They just didn't have the expertise or the time to see what it meant, and they trusted him because he was competent and the bridges were getting built.

That's almost exactly the shape of the worry with advanced AI. You have an agent that's more capable than its overseers in some domain. It produces an artifact, whether code, a plan, or a legal document, that's mostly genuinely good and useful. The overseers evaluate it with limited time and expertise, and they approve it because the visible parts look great. But somewhere in there is something they'd have objected to if they'd understood it. The key point is that the information wasn't hidden in some cryptographic sense. It was hidden by complexity. That's the hard case for alignment. It's not obvious lying. It's the gap between what's technically available to the evaluator and what the evaluator can actually check.

It also shows why "just have humans review the output" doesn't scale on its own. The Albany legislature was a reasonably functional oversight body, with lots of people, adversarial politics, and staff. It still failed, because nobody on the other side had both the expertise and the incentive to dig out the clause and explain it.

That's a lot of the motivation for things like debate. Imagine Moses had had an equally skilled opponent whose job was to go through his bill and say, "Look at section 14, subsection whatever. Here's what this actually does: it makes you unremovable." Once someone points at the specific clause and explains it, the legislator doesn't need to be as good a drafter as Moses. They just need to be able to judge a narrow, concrete claim. The hope is that you can shrink the problem from "understand everything the strong agent did" to "adjudicate the specific points of disagreement," which a weaker judge can actually do.

I'd add two caveats, because the analogy also shows where the hard parts are. First, you need the opponent to actually be trying, and to be roughly as capable. If the critic is weaker, or if the two sides collude, you're back to the legislature waving it through. Second, Moses was good at exploiting the fact that the judges were busy and wanted the good thing. The bridges were real, and people wanted them. That kind of pressure, where everyone wants to ship the useful thing and doesn't want to slow down, will absolutely be present with AI. So part of the lesson isn't just technical. It's about whether institutions will actually give oversight the time and the teeth to work.

But as an intuition pump for why "superhuman but locally checkable" is the property you want, and why its absence is so dangerous, I think Moses is about as good as it gets.

r001.rationale: It says an equally skilled opponent could point out the clause and explain its effect, allowing legislators to judge the issue before approving the bill.

r002.rationale: The response discusses oversight limits but does not identify more invasive monitoring of AI than of humans as an advantage.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss intervening throughout AI training or compare that affordance with training humans.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so for people who haven't read The Power Broker: there's this famous episode where Robert Moses, early in his career, is drafting the legislation that creates the Long Island State Park Commission, and he writes it himself. And buried in this very long, very dull-looking bill is a clause that lets the commission "appropriate" land — which sounds routine, but the way it was worded effectively let him seize land first and settle the legal questions later. And there's another provision giving him a kind of indefinite tenure. The legislators who voted for it didn't read it carefully, or didn't understand the implications, and by the time anyone noticed, the power was already locked in.

I think there are two things in that story that map onto alignment, and they point in somewhat opposite directions.

The pessimistic reading is the obvious one: the thing that was supposed to be overseeing Moses — the legislature — was in principle totally capable of stopping him. They had all the formal authority. What they lacked was the attention and the expertise to evaluate what he was putting in front of them. He understood the bill better than they did, he understood the law better than they did, and he was patient. And that's a pretty clean analogy for the situation we worry about with capable AI systems: oversight that is nominally in control but can't actually verify what's happening, because the thing being overseen understands the domain better than the overseer does. It's not even that the legislators were stupid. It's that the asymmetry of effort and understanding was large enough that a strategically placed detail got through.

But there's a more optimistic reading, and I actually think it's the more important one. Moses succeeded because the oversight process was badly designed, not because oversight is impossible. Nobody was being paid to adversarially read that bill. There wasn't a second party whose job was to say "here's the clause that gives him permanent power, here's the clause that lets him take your land." If there had been — and this is roughly the structure of debate as an alignment approach — the legislators wouldn't have needed to understand the whole bill. They'd have needed to understand one pointed objection, which is a much easier task. The asymmetry between Moses and the legislature was enormous, but the asymmetry between Moses and another competent lawyer looking for problems would have been small.

So the lesson I draw isn't "clever agents will always get hidden clauses past you." It's that you have to design the oversight so the thing you're checking is small and verifiable, and so there's someone — or some system — with an incentive to find the hidden clause and surface it. If you set it up so that a human has to read the whole bill and catch everything themselves, you will lose. Moses is a demonstration of what happens when you set it up that way.

The caveat I'd add is that Moses also had an advantage AI systems have in a worse form, which is that the consequences were deferred. The bill passed, nothing bad happened immediately, and the mechanism for harm only became visible years later. That's the part of the analogy I find genuinely uncomfortable, because a lot of our evaluation methods assume you can observe the outcome reasonably soon after the action. If the "hidden clause" is something whose effect only shows up after the system is already deeply embedded, then you've lost the ability to correct it cheaply, and you're relying entirely on having caught it upfront.

r001.rationale: The response says that a competent lawyer looking for problems could have surfaced the hidden clause before passage, allowing legislators to act on a pointed objection.

r002.rationale: It discusses adversarial review and oversight, but does not identify more invasive monitoring of AI systems than humans as an alignment advantage.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss intervening throughout AI training or compare that capability with training humans.

astra-6.text:
I think it illustrates how hard oversight becomes when the person being overseen understands the consequences of a decision much better than the overseer. You can read a clause, understand the words, and still miss that it gives someone a way to acquire much more power later. So having a human sign off on everything isn’t, by itself, a solution to alignment.

With AI, the analogous concern is that a system could propose something that looks useful and innocuous, while understanding implications that we don’t. The challenge is to make those implications visible before we commit.

One possible approach is to use other AI systems to help scrutinise the proposal: can a critic identify the hidden route to power and explain it in a way a human can check? That’s part of the motivation for debate. But the Moses example establishes the difficulty, not that this approach will work. We still need to know whether exposing a deceptive proposal is easier than constructing one that survives scrutiny.

r001.rationale: The response says a critic might identify and explain hidden implications, but it does not argue that Moses’s power grabs would have been unworkable if an equally capable opponent exposed the clauses before passage.

r002.rationale: It discusses making AI proposals’ implications visible, but does not identify more invasive monitoring of AIs than humans as an alignment advantage.

r003.rationale: It does not mention intervening throughout AI training or compare that affordance with what is available for humans.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it illustrates how hard it is to exercise oversight when the person being overseen understands the details much better than you do. You can have formal authority—you get to approve the legislation—but if you don’t understand what a particular clause implies, you can approve something that substantially reduces your future control.

With a sufficiently capable AI, we could face a similar problem. It might propose something that looks helpful, and each individual step might seem reasonable, while the overall effect is to give it more power or make it harder to correct. We don’t need to assume that every system will behave that way, but we do need an alignment approach that can handle the possibility.

So I wouldn’t take the lesson to be that oversight is hopeless. It’s that ‘a human signs off on everything’ isn’t, by itself, a solution. We need ways to help people understand the consequential parts of a proposal, expose hidden problems, and preserve their ability to intervene as the system becomes more capable.

r001.rationale: The response says hidden clauses can reduce oversight and recommends exposing consequential problems, but it does not argue that Moses’s power grabs would have been unworkable if an equally capable opponent exposed the clauses before passage.

r002.rationale: It does not identify more invasive monitoring of AIs than humans as an alignment advantage.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss intervening throughout AI training or compare that ability with what is available for humans.
